Each household member (Joseph, Ann, Sarah, Joseph Jr.) matched exactly on name, birth year, and birthplace across both 1860 and 1880 censuses. The same_person scores (0.78 strong band) were obtained for all primary assertions and properly recorded. The LDS emigration corridor from Liverpool was correctly identified via wiki_read and cited in every rationale. Residence facts were materialized with proper source references (S10, S11). No fabricated claims or unsupported assertions.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Completeness
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: All 18 assertions from both census records were linked to the correct tree persons. The 1860 census yielded 9 assertions (4 persons × name/birth + 1 residence) all linked; the 1880 census yielded 9 assertions (3 persons × name/birth + 1 residence + 2 relationship assertions) all linked. Both relationship assertions (wife, son) were linked to both parties as required. Sarah Pratt's absence from 1880 was flagged as a follow-up question. No assertions were left unlinked or unaddressed.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. research_query calls retrieved assertions by sourceId (src_001, src_002). tree_query retrieved the existing tree. place_search calls used placeName arguments matching Cranfield and Salt Lake County. place_distance compared the two standardized places correctly. wiki_read accessed the Utah_Emigration_and_Immigration page. same_person calls paired each primary assertion with the correct tree person (a_001→I1, a_003→I2, a_005→I3, a_007→I4, a_010→I1, a_012→I2, a_014→I4, a_017→I1 and I2, a_018→I1 and I4). materialize_facts enriched all four persons with residence facts from both records. No calls returned fixture_not_found errors. One validation rejection on the second research_append batch was immediately corrected with proper same_person calls for a_017 and a_018.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: All 20 person_evidence entries correctly scored as 'confident'. The identity evidence is strong: exact name matches, exact birth year matches (~1822, ~1825, ~1847, ~1850), England birthplace corroboration, and household composition agreement across two independent censuses (1860 and 1880) provide multiple independent sources. The same_person score of 0.78 (strong band) on every pairing supports confidence. The geographic move from Cranfield, Bedfordshire to Salt Lake County (~7,767 km) is bridged by the documented LDS emigration corridor naming Liverpool as the departure port and New York/Philadelphia/Boston as arrival ports (1855-1890 era), which explains the move without contradiction. No chronological gaps or qualitative conflicts exist. Confidence tier matches identity-evidence strength.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Rationale quality
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Every rationale cites specific matching attributes: name (exact match), birth year (gap 0 years), birthplace (England compatible with Cranfield, Bedfordshire, England), and household composition (wife Ann, children Sarah and Joseph with matching names and ages). Each rationale explicitly names the LDS emigration corridor from the wiki page ('Many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England' with era 1840–1890). The move is explained by reference to documented historical migration patterns, not left as an unexplained gap. Rationales address why competing candidates were ruled out by noting the exact household fit and corroboration across two censuses. The move_bridge field documents the corridor source.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: All relationship-implying assertions were linked to both parties. The 1880 census relationship assertions (a_017 'wife of Joseph Pratt' and a_018 'son of Joseph Pratt') each generated two person_evidence entries: one for the named party (I2 Ann, I4 Joseph Jr.) and one for the implied other party (I1 Joseph as husband/father). pe_015 and pe_016 both link a_017 (to I2 and I1 respectively); pe_019 and pe_020 both link a_018 (to I4 and I1 respectively). No relationship assertion was left with only one-side linking.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all four census personas matched existing tree persons (I1, I2, I3, I4). materialize_facts was called twice (once for 1860 record with 4 persons, once for 1880 record with 3 persons) to enrich existing persons with sourced residence facts from the census records. Each call succeeded with proper source references attached (S10 for 1860, S11 for 1880). The 1860 and 1880 records are household censuses, so edges (couple/parent-child relationships) are not owed by person-evidence; they already exist in the tree (R1 couple, R2-R5 parent-child). No edges were written by person-evidence, which is correct for this scenario. No merge_warnings dry-run was needed because no new persons were created. All existing tree persons were left unexplained-absence-free except Sarah (I3), whose absence from 1880 was flagged as a follow-up question, not overwritten.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Score discipline
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every primary assertion and relationship assertion where a tree candidate existed. For the 1860 census: a_001 (I1), a_003 (I2), a_005 (I3), a_007 (I4) each scored 0.78. For the 1880 census: a_010 (I1), a_012 (I2), a_014 (I4) each scored 0.78. Relationship assertions a_017 and a_018 were scored for both parties (a_017→I1 and I2; a_018→I1 and I4). Each score was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision without overriding it. The high score (0.78 strong band) combined with strong qualitative correlation (exact name, age, birthplace, household fit) and the documented LDS corridor justifies 'confident' on every link. No score was inverted or misapplied. recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party (e.g., a_017 is about the wife, so recordRole 'head' was supplied only for the I1 link, not the I2 link).

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Each link is supported by multiple independent corroborating factors: (1) exact name matches (Hermann Gaetjen, Amelia Nichols, Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen); (2) family structure corroboration (the record names the bride's parents as Hermann and Amelia, matching I1 and I4's known relationship and I3's known parentage); (3) geographic consistency (all San Francisco, matching the family cluster); (4) same_person scores of 0.95–0.97, indicating strong record-to-tree alignment; (5) chronological consistency (no contradictions; the 1-year birth gap for I3 is within self-reporting noise on a marriage certificate). No warnings for either pre-existing person.

---

Here is a summary of what was matched and built from the 1850 Schuylkill County census of the Thomas Flynn household.

Thomas Flynn, the household head, was already linked to his tree entry as a probable match — his name and location fit well, and nothing contradicts the connection. Two children were listed in the census: John Flynn (about age 8, born around 1842 in Ireland) and Bridget Flynn (about age 6, born around 1844 in Ireland). Neither John nor Bridget was in the tree before. Both were added as new family members and are now linked to the census as probable matches, based on their household position directly under Thomas and their shared surname. Because each is introduced by a single record with no independent confirmation yet, the match level is "probably" rather than "certainly."

One notable absence: Patrick Flynn, who is already recorded in the tree as Thomas's son and was born around 1845, does not appear in this census household at all. This could mean he died before 1850, was recorded elsewhere on census day, was simply missed by the enumerator, or — less likely given the other evidence — this household belongs to a different Thomas Flynn. This absence deserves a follow-up search, particularly a death search for Patrick before 1850 and a check of neighboring households in the same census. That search is the natural next step.

output.text_response:
Here is what the **person-evidence** agent found and did:

---

## Linking Complete — William Weller Household

All five household members were matched to existing tree persons (no stubs needed), with **22 person_evidence entries created** across both censuses.

### Persons Linked

| Tree Person | Role in 1870 | Role in 1880 |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| **I1 — William Weller** | Head | Head |
| **I2 — Mary Weller** | Member | Wife |
| **I3 — James Weller** | Member | *(absent — see note)* |
| **I4 — Ellen Weller** | Member | *(absent — see note)* |
| **I5 — George Weller** | Member | Son |

All links are rated **"probable" (score 0.78/1.0)** — the names, ages, birthplaces, and family structure match across both censuses, but no transatlantic voyage or naturalization record has been found yet to explain how the family moved from Horsham, Sussex, England (last placed there in 1861) to Tennessee. That gap prevents an upgrade to "confident."

---

### Notable Finding — James & Ellen Missing from 1880

James (I3, ~28 in 1880) and Ellen (I4, ~25 in 1880) appear in the 1870 household but not the 1880 one. Likely explanations: married and established separate households, enumerated elsewhere, or died before 1880. This is a natural next research question.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Search for a **passenger list or naturalization record** documenting the Wellers' crossing from England to the United States. Finding it would both confirm the identification and allow confidence levels to be upgraded from "probable" to "confident." After that, tracking down James and Ellen in the 1880 census would round out the family picture.
